splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on when actuarial assumptions used to calculate employer withdrawal liability under ERISA must be finalized. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers participating in multiemployer pension plans, as the timing directly controls how much withdrawing employers must pay.

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that the plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, allowing plans flexibility in choosing assumptions that reflect more current conditions.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions must be fixed by the end of the prior plan year (the statutory measurement date), providing employers with greater predictability about potential liability.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. The outcome affects how federal courts calculate sentencing at revocation hearings for thousands of individuals who abscond each year.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the supervised release term is tolled during the period a supervisee is a fugitive, extending the court's authority to revoke supervised release beyond the original term.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that without explicit statutory authorization, courts may not toll the supervised release term when a supervisee absconds, as doing so exceeds judicial authority to extend punishment.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face the stricter gatekeeping requirement of Section 2244(b)(1) — which categorically bars any previously presented claim — in addition to Section 2255(h)'s requirements. This determines whether federal prisoners must show newly discovered evidence or a new constitutional rule, or are entirely barred from raising previously presented claims.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the categorical bar on relitigating previously raised claims under § 2244(b)(1) applies to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, imposing an additional gatekeeping requirement beyond § 2255(h).

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of showing newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law, without the additional categorical bar of § 2244(b)(1).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the standing requirements for candidates challenging election administration rules before an election takes place. The outcome affects whether pre-election challenges to voting procedures are viable or whether such disputes can only be raised post-election, with significant implications for election administration nationwide.

positions.label: Candidate has standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates have Article III standing to challenge state election laws pre-election based on competitive injury from allegedly unlawful voting procedures.

positions.label: Candidate lacks standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate's generalized interest in election integrity, without a concrete and particularized injury, is insufficient to confer Article III standing for pre-election challenges.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any one criterion disqualifies).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria or if possessing any one is disqualifying. This governs whether district courts must impose sentences without regard to statutory minimums and leads to disparate sentencing across the country.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), reading 'and' in its ordinary conjunctive sense.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1) disqualifies a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as 'or' in context.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes precedence over agency or Sentencing Commission deference when interpreting ambiguous criminal sentencing provisions.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether lenity trumps deference to the Sentencing Commission's (or an agency's) interpretation of ambiguous criminal provisions. The Third Circuit held that agency deference trumps lenity, while the Fourth, Fifth, and Eleventh Circuits hold that lenity prevails. This affects how ambiguous sentencing enhancements are resolved.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes precedence over agency or Sentencing Commission deference in criminal contexts, requiring ambiguous provisions to be resolved in the defendant's favor.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that deference to agency or Sentencing Commission interpretations prevails over the rule of lenity, allowing anti-defendant readings of ambiguous criminal provisions to stand when supported by authoritative commentary.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' in U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) includes inchoate offenses like conspiracy, based on Application Note 1's expansion of the guideline text.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether Application Note 1 to the career-offender guideline — which adds conspiracy and other inchoate offenses to the definition of 'controlled substance offense' — is a valid, binding interpretation of the guideline text under Stinson and Kisor. This determines whether defendants with prior conspiracy convictions qualify as career offenders.

positions.label: Commentary validly includes inchoate offenses
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is an authoritative interpretation of the career-offender guideline that validly expands 'controlled substance offense' to include conspiracy, and defers to the Sentencing Commission's interpretation under Stinson/Kisor.

positions.label: Commentary impermissibly expands guideline text
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses and that Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the definition beyond its plain meaning, so conspiracy convictions cannot serve as career-offender predicates.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state-controlled substance is not on the federal schedules.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the underlying substance to be federally scheduled. The Eighth Circuit holds there is no federal-law limitation, while other circuits have required the substance to appear on federal schedules. This affects career-offender and other enhancement determinations.

positions.label: No federal-schedule limitation
positions.summary: Holds that the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' encompasses state drug offenses regardless of whether the substance is federally controlled, finding no textual basis to graft a federal-law limitation onto the guideline.

positions.label: Federal-schedule limitation applies
positions.summary: Holds that a prior state conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Guidelines only if the substance is also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether non-retroactive changes in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), can constitute or contribute to 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits are sharply divided on whether courts may consider non-retroactive legal changes as a basis for compassionate release. Several circuits prohibit it entirely, while others allow it as one factor among many. This affects thousands of federal prisoners serving sentences under outdated sentencing regimes.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, whether alone or combined with other factors, cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may be considered
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider non-retroactive changes in law as one factor among others when evaluating whether extraordinary and compelling reasons warrant a sentence reduction.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of an asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to debtors who convert from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 in good faith under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value between the filing of a Chapter 13 petition and a good-faith conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor. The Ninth Circuit held it belongs to the estate, creating a split with other circuits that protect debtors' post-petition appreciation upon conversion.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation in property value belongs to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7, based on the broad scope of § 541(a).

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that § 348(f)(1)(A) protects good-faith converting debtors by limiting the converted estate to the value of property as of the original petition date, so post-petition appreciation remains with the debtor.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners must bring challenges to conditions of confinement (as opposed to the fact or duration of confinement) through habeas corpus or may use civil rights actions such as Bivens.
splits.description: Since Preiser v. Rodriguez, circuits have disagreed on whether conditions-of-confinement claims by prisoners are cognizable only in habeas or may also be brought as civil rights claims. This longstanding split affects prisoners' ability to challenge BOP decisions regarding First Step Act time credits and prerelease custody.

positions.label: Habeas is the exclusive remedy
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to conditions of confinement that affect the duration or execution of a sentence must be brought through habeas corpus, not civil rights actions.

positions.label: Civil rights actions are also available
positions.summary: Holds that prisoners may use civil rights actions (§ 1983 or Bivens) to challenge conditions of confinement even when the challenge may also implicate the duration of confinement.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the civil or criminal deadline for filing a notice of appeal applies to an order on a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees in a criminal case.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter (with a 30-day appeal deadline) or part of the criminal case (with a 14-day deadline). The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies, but at least one circuit applies the criminal deadline.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion is part of the criminal case, so the 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b) applies.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release at revocation proceedings, or whether revocation sentences must be based solely on the breach of the court's trust.
splits.description: The Sixth Circuit allows district courts to punish defendants for the conduct underlying supervised release violations, placing it at the extreme end of a circuit split. Other circuits hold that revocation sentences should reflect the breach of trust, not serve as additional punishment for the underlying conduct.

positions.label: Punishment for violation conduct is permissible
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly punish defendants for the conduct underlying their supervised release violations, not just for the breach of trust in violating release conditions.

positions.label: Revocation is about breach of trust, not punishment
positions.summary: Holds that the purpose of supervised release revocation is to sanction the breach of the court's trust inherent in the defendant's violation, not to impose additional punishment for the underlying conduct.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments under 42 U.S.C. § 1981 or analogous federal law?
splits.description: The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve disagreement among circuits about the standards for discrimination claims in business and hospitality settings. The Second Circuit's approach was found sufficiently unsettled to warrant review, suggesting a circuit split on the applicable legal framework for liability and damages.

positions.label: Broader liability standards
positions.summary: Applies a more plaintiff-friendly standard for establishing discrimination claims in hospitality or business settings, allowing claims to proceed with less direct evidence of discriminatory intent.

positions.label: Narrower liability standards
positions.summary: Applies a more restrictive standard for discrimination claims in business establishments, requiring stronger evidence of intentional discrimination.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether claims that could also be raised in habeas proceedings — such as alleged legal errors in the underlying conviction — may be considered by district courts evaluating compassionate release motions. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors while others hold they are categorically excluded from the compassionate release analysis.

positions.label: May consider conviction-related errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider factors related to potential errors in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: May not consider conviction-related errors
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to the validity of a conviction or sentence are categorically excluded from the compassionate release framework and must be raised through habeas corpus.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which bars states from enacting or enforcing laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any . . . broker,' preempts state negligence claims arising from a freight broker's selection of a motor carrier. This question affects liability in the trucking industry where brokers play a significant intermediary role.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted because they relate to the broker's 'service' of arranging transportation, which falls within the FAAAA's preemption clause.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers for negligent hiring of motor carriers are not preempted because they do not directly regulate brokers' prices, routes, or services within the meaning of the FAAAA.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to a person who uses marijuana.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass'n v. Bruen, circuits have split on whether the federal prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users — particularly marijuana users — is consistent with the Second Amendment's text and historical tradition of firearms regulation.

positions.label: § 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) does not violate the Second Amendment because the historical tradition of firearms regulation supports disarming individuals whose drug use renders them dangerous or irresponsible.

positions.label: § 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a sufficient historical analogue justifying the disarmament of non-violent drug users.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the Section 1 exemption for transportation workers, particularly whether last-mile delivery workers who distribute goods to retail stores are 'engaged in . . . interstate commerce.' This affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a wide range of distribution workers.

positions.label: Broad exemption — last-mile delivery workers qualify
positions.summary: Holds that workers who are part of a continuous interstate transportation chain, including those making last-mile deliveries of goods that have moved in interstate commerce, qualify as transportation workers exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow exemption — last-mile distributors do not qualify
positions.summary: Holds that distribution workers delivering goods locally to retail stores are not 'transportation workers engaged in . . . interstate commerce' under Section 1 because they are not themselves moving goods across state lines.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: The circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claims are based on labeling that the EPA approved. This affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticides nationwide.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would require labeling different from or in addition to what the EPA has approved.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because they impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements, consistent with the Supreme Court's Bates v. Dow Agrosciences framework.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether RLUIPA creates a cause of action for money damages against state prison officials in their individual capacities. Some circuits have held that RLUIPA, enacted under the Spending Clause, does not clearly authorize personal-liability damages against individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds, while others have allowed such claims to proceed.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA provides a cause of action for money damages against state prison officials sued in their individual capacities for violations of prisoners' religious exercise rights.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials because Congress cannot impose personal liability on non-recipient individuals through the Spending Clause.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
